course.title: JDBC-shaped data access in plain Java
course.description: Data access against the real java.sql interfaces, faked in memory: bind parameters and LIKE escapes, a transaction template, chunked batches, two queries instead of N+1, SQL NULL versus zero, and optimistic updates that check the row count (JDK 17).

unit.title: Build a filtered query with parameters, IN lists and LIKE escapes
Commit, roll back, and never lose the first exception
Insert in batches, and do not drop the last one
Load orders and their lines in two queries, not N+1
Map a row where NULL is not zero
An optimistic update that checks its row count

javadrills/14-jdbc-data-access/01-parame.instructions:
**Skills:** JDBC · SQL injection · dynamic queries  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "The order search builds its SQL with string concatenation. A customer called O'Brien gets a 500, and searching for `50%` returns every order. Rewrite the builder."

**Why it matters.** Values belong in bind parameters, never in the SQL text: then a quote is just a character and nothing the user types can change the query. Two cases need care. An `IN` list needs one `?` per value (and an empty list must match nothing, not become `IN ()`, which is a syntax error). A `LIKE` pattern is a parameter too, but `%` and `_` inside it are still wildcards, so user text is escaped before the `%...%` is added.

**Your task.** Implement `static Sql findOrders(Filter f)` returning the SQL text and its parameters in order:
- start with `SELECT id, customer, status, total_cents FROM orders`
- conditions, each only when its filter is non-null, joined with ` AND ` after ` WHERE `, in this order:
  - `nameContains`: `LOWER(customer) LIKE ? ESCAPE '!'` with the parameter `%<text>%`, where the text is lower-cased (`Locale.ROOT`) and each `!`, `%` and `_` in it is prefixed with `!`
  - `statuses`: `status IN (?, ?, ...)` with one parameter per status; an EMPTY list gives the condition `1 = 0` and no parameter
  - `minTotalCents`: `total_cents >= ?`
- end with ` ORDER BY id LIMIT ?` and `limit` as the last parameter; a limit outside 1..100 is refused with `IllegalArgumentException`

**Worked example.** `Filter("O'Brien", List.of("PAID", "SHIPPED"), null, 20)` gives `... WHERE LOWER(customer) LIKE ? ESCAPE '!' AND status IN (?, ?) ORDER BY id LIMIT ?` with `[%o'brien%, PAID, SHIPPED, 20]`.
hints: Nothing the user types should ever become part of the SQL text. Even inside a parameter, two characters keep a special meaning for LIKE.

Build a list of conditions and a list of parameters together, adding one placeholder per IN value and treating an empty list as a condition that is never true. Escape the escape character before the wildcards.

Lower-case the search text, prefix the escape character, the percent sign and the underscore with the escape character, wrap it in percent signs as a parameter, and join the conditions with AND before the ordering and the limit.

javadrills/14-jdbc-data-access/02-a-tran.instructions:
**Skills:** JDBC · transactions · exception handling  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "A failed transfer left the connection in manual-commit mode, and the next request on that pooled connection silently never committed. Another time the log showed 'rollback failed' and nobody knew what had gone wrong first."

**Why it matters.** With plain JDBC you own the transaction: turn auto-commit off, commit on success, roll back on ANY failure, and give the connection back the way you found it, because a pool will hand it to the next caller. If the rollback fails too, the first exception is the one that explains the problem; the rollback failure travels with it as a suppressed exception instead of replacing it.

**Your task.** Implement `static <T> T inTransaction(Connection c, Work<T> work) throws SQLException`:
- remember `c.getAutoCommit()`, then turn auto-commit off
- run `work`; on success commit and return its result
- if `work` throws an `SQLException` or a `RuntimeException`: roll back and rethrow that same exception; if the rollback throws, add its exception to the original as suppressed
- in every case, set auto-commit back to the value it had before
- do not close the connection: the caller owns it

**Worked example.** A work that runs one update and returns 1 leaves the log `[autoCommit=false, update ..., commit, autoCommit=true]`.
hints: Three things must happen on different exits. One only on success, one only on failure, and one always.

Remember the auto-commit setting, switch it off, commit after the work, roll back when it fails and attach a failed rollback to the original exception, and restore the setting in a block that always runs.

Read the old auto-commit value, disable it, run and commit in the try, roll back in a multi-catch for SQL and runtime exceptions adding any rollback exception as suppressed before rethrowing, and restore the old value in finally.

javadrills/14-jdbc-data-access/03-batch-.instructions:
**Skills:** JDBC · batching · off-by-one  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Importing 10,000 rows one `executeUpdate` at a time takes minutes. Batch it, but our last attempt lost the final few rows of every file."

**Why it matters.** A JDBC batch sends many parameter sets in one round trip. Large imports send it in chunks so neither the driver nor the database holds everything at once. The classic bug executes the batch only when the counter reaches the chunk size, so the last partial chunk is never sent. All chunks belong to one transaction: either the whole file is imported or none of it.

**Your task.** Implement `static int insertAll(Connection c, List<Row> rows, int chunk) throws SQLException` with the given `INSERT_SQL` (`sku`, `qty`):
- `chunk < 1`: `IllegalArgumentException`
- no rows: return 0 without preparing or executing anything
- otherwise, in one transaction (auto-commit off, one commit at the end, auto-commit restored): one prepared statement, parameters per row, `addBatch`, and `executeBatch` every `chunk` rows and once more for any remainder; never execute an empty batch
- return the number of rows inserted (the sum of the counts `executeBatch` returned)
- on an `SQLException`: roll back, restore auto-commit, rethrow

**Worked example.** 5 rows with `chunk = 2` send batches of 2, 2 and 1 and commit once.
hints: Count rows since the last flush. When the loop ends, that count is not always zero.

Prepare one statement, add each row to the batch and execute it whenever a full chunk is waiting, then execute once more only if rows are still waiting. Do all of it between turning auto-commit off and a single commit.

Guard the chunk size and the empty list first, then in a transaction add rows to the batch, execute when the pending count reaches the chunk and after the loop when it is above zero, sum the counts, and roll back on an SQL exception.

javadrills/14-jdbc-data-access/04-two-qu.instructions:
**Skills:** JDBC · N+1 · query budgets  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "The order history page runs 201 queries for a customer with 200 orders. Get it to two, and keep it under the database's limit on bind parameters."

**Why it matters.** Loading each order's lines with its own query is N+1: one query for the orders, one per order for the lines. One query with `WHERE order_id IN (...)` fetches every line, and grouping in Java puts each line under its order. Databases cap the number of bind parameters in one statement, so a long id list is sent in chunks: the budget becomes 1 + ceil(N / chunk) queries instead of 1 + N.

**Your task.** Implement `static List<OrderView> ordersWithLines(Connection c, String customer, int maxIds) throws SQLException`:
- run `ORDERS_SQL` with `customer`; it returns columns `id` (long) in id order
- no orders: return an empty list after that one query
- otherwise load the lines with `SELECT order_id, sku, qty FROM order_lines WHERE order_id IN (?, ?, ...) ORDER BY order_id, sku`, at most `maxIds` ids per query (one `?` per id, ids in order, chunks in order)
- return one `OrderView(id, lines)` per order, in order; each `lines` list in the order the rows came back; an order without lines gets an empty list

**Worked example.** Orders 1, 2, 3 with `maxIds = 2` run three queries: the orders, `IN (?, ?)` with `[1, 2]`, and `IN (?)` with `[3]`.
hints: Every order's lines can come back from one statement. The only limit is how many ids one statement may carry.

Read the order ids first, then for each slice of at most the allowed size build a statement with one placeholder per id and add every returned line to its order, which you prepared with an empty list.

Collect the ids, stop early when there are none, loop over sublists of the allowed size issuing one IN query each with the ids bound in order, and append each line to the list of the order whose id the row names.

javadrills/14-jdbc-data-access/05-sql-nu.instructions:
**Skills:** JDBC · ResultSet · null handling  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Customers without a discount show '0% off' and some get the zero-discount promotion email. The column is nullable; the mapper uses `rs.getInt("discount_pct")`."

**Why it matters.** `ResultSet.getInt`, `getLong` and the other primitive getters return `0` for SQL `NULL`; only a following `rs.wasNull()` (or `rs.getObject(label, Integer.class)`, which returns `null`) tells the two apart. Object getters such as `getString` and `getBigDecimal` return `null` directly. A zero discount and no discount are different facts, so the record uses `Integer`.

**Your task.** Implement `static Customer map(ResultSet rs)` for the current row and `static List<Customer> readAll(ResultSet rs)` for every row:
- `id` (BIGINT NOT NULL), `name` (VARCHAR NOT NULL), `discount_pct` (INT NULL), `credit_limit` (DECIMAL NULL)
- SQL `NULL` in a nullable column becomes `null` in the record; a real `0` stays `0`
- `readAll` advances with `rs.next()` and maps each row, in order; no rows give an empty list

**Worked example.** A row `{id: 7, name: "Ana", discount_pct: NULL, credit_limit: 250.00}` maps to `Customer[id=7, name=Ana, discountPct=null, creditLimit=250.00]`.
hints: A primitive int cannot be null, so the driver needs another way to tell you a value was missing.
Read the discount with the int getter and ask the result set straight after whether that value was SQL NULL, or ask for the column as an Integer object. The object getters already give null.

Call the int getter for the discount and immediately check was-null to decide between null and the number, take the decimal and the strings from their object getters, and loop over next to collect every row.

javadrills/14-jdbc-data-access/06-check-.instructions:
**Skills:** JDBC · optimistic locking · lost updates  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Two support agents edit the same customer; the second save silently wins and the first agent's change is gone. The table has a `version` column nobody checks."

**Why it matters.** Optimistic locking puts the version you read into the `WHERE` clause and bumps it in the same statement. If someone else saved first, the row no longer has that version and the update touches 0 rows. `executeUpdate` returns that count; ignoring it turns a detected conflict back into a lost update.

**Your task.** Implement `static long rename(Connection c, long id, long expectedVersion, String newName) throws SQLException` with the given `RENAME_SQL`:
- bind `newName`, `id`, `expectedVersion`, in that order, and run the update
- 1 row: return the new version (`expectedVersion + 1`)
- 0 rows: throw `StaleUpdate` with the message `customer <id> changed since version <expectedVersion>`
- more than 1 row: throw `IllegalStateException` (the id is not unique: never ignore it)
- a blank or null `newName` is refused with `IllegalArgumentException` before any SQL runs

**Worked example.** `rename(c, 7, 3, "Ana Lima")` sends `[Ana Lima, 7, 3]`; if the fake answers 1 row the result is 4, if it answers 0 the caller gets `StaleUpdate("customer 7 changed since version 3")`.
hints: The database already told you whether the version still matched. Look at what executing the update hands back.
Refuse a blank name first, bind the three values in the order of the placeholders, run the update and turn zero rows into a stale-update error and more than one row into an illegal-state error.

Validate the name, prepare the given statement, set the name, the id and the expected version as parameters one to three, execute, branch on the row count, and give back the expected version plus one.
